quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Readers, Purpose, and Structure
quizzes.intro: Check whether you understand reader-first writing, the clarity stack, and scannable structure.

questions.prompt: How does workplace writing differ from much school writing?

options.text: It rewards maximum length and mystery
It rewards decisions and action for interrupted readers
It forbids any structure
It never becomes a record

questions.explanation: Work writing serves busy readers who must decide or act, and it often becomes institutional memory.

wrongExplanations.a: Length and mystery are usually liabilities.
wrongExplanations.d: Email and docs often become records.

questions.prompt: What should you define before drafting?

options.text: How many buzzwords to include
The reader, their job-to-be-done, and the outcome after reading
A sarcastic tone for the archive
Whether to hide the ask forever

questions.explanation: Reader-first planning prevents journaling disguised as communication.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best matches the clarity stack?

options.text: Purpose, point, proof, ask, next step
Joke, suspense, apology, silence
Attachments first, purpose never
Jargon, ego, buried ask

questions.explanation: Purpose and point lead; proof supports; ask and next step close the loop.

wrongExplanations.b: That is entertainment, not work clarity.

options.text: Quick question
Need approval: vendor quote for staging servers by Thu 3pm
Hi

questions.explanation: Subject lines should promise the content and often include the ask and timing.

wrongExplanations.a: Too vague for search and priority.

questions.prompt: Why prefer active voice as a default?

options.text: Because passive voice is illegal
Because active sentences usually clarify who does what
Because active voice hides owners
Because readers dislike short sentences always

questions.explanation: Active voice makes agency and responsibility easier to see.

wrongExplanations.a: Passive voice is allowed when useful; it is not illegal.
wrongExplanations.c: Hiding owners is a problem passive fog can cause.
wrongExplanations.d: Short clear sentences are often welcome.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Emails, Tone, and Editing
quizzes.intro: Apply email structure, status writing, tone, hedging, and editing discipline.

questions.prompt: Where should the ask usually appear in a work email?

options.text: Buried after a long personal narrative
Early—often in the first lines with purpose
Only in an attachment filename
Never; readers should guess

questions.explanation: Busy readers need the ask findable in seconds.

wrongExplanations.a: Buried asks are a top failure mode.

questions.prompt: Which status format aligns with the lesson?

options.text: A full diary of every minute
Clear signal such as Done/Doing/Blocked/Ask or RAG plus risk and decision needed
No updates until crisis
Only emojis without owners

questions.explanation: Status writing should provide signal, risks, and asks—not noise.

options.text: Whenever you want to avoid owning a clear recommendation you actually have
When uncertainty is real and honesty requires nuance
In every sentence as a style flex
Never, even when facts are unknown

questions.explanation: Hedges serve truth; they should not replace courage when a recommendation is warranted.

wrongExplanations.d: False certainty is also a problem.

options.text: Can I add more buzzwords?
Is the ask findable in about ten seconds?
Did I remove all deadlines on purpose?
Did I hide the owners?

questions.explanation: The ten-second ask test is a practical clarity gate.

options.text: I was wondering if perhaps we might potentially revisit the timeline given various concerns.
I recommend moving the launch to May 12 because Legal needs two review days. Can you approve by Friday?
Timeline stuff TBD somehow.
Per my last vibe check…

questions.explanation: The clear version states recommendation, reason, and ask with timing.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Genres, Norms, and Judgment
quizzes.intro: Use the full lesson. Focus on feedback, medium choice, inclusivity, and professional judgment.

options.text: Vague insults about quality
Specific behavioral notes with impact and a clear request
Public sarcasm
No examples and no next step

questions.explanation: Usable feedback is specific, impact-aware, and actionable.

wrongExplanations.c: Sarcasm harms trust, especially in writing.

questions.prompt: When might a meeting beat a long email?

options.text: Never; writing always wins
When the topic is emotionally sensitive or needs rapid interactive clarification
When you want no record of decisions ever
When a simple FYI would have been enough

questions.explanation: Medium selection is part of craft; talk first for some conflicts, write for many updates.

wrongExplanations.a: Medium depends on stakes and content.

questions.prompt: Which practice supports inclusive workplace writing?

options.text: Heavy idioms and unexplained acronyms for global audiences
Plain language, defined acronyms, and descriptive links
Gendered assumptions when irrelevant
Tiny walls of text without headings

questions.explanation: Accessibility and inclusion start with plain, explicit language.

wrongExplanations.c: Irrelevant gendered language should be avoided.
wrongExplanations.d: Walls of text hurt scanning for everyone.

questions.prompt: How should you replace ‘ASAP’ in most cases?

options.text: With more exclamation marks
With a specific day and time, or a true flexible window
With silence about timing
With ‘whenever’ and hidden urgency later

questions.explanation: Precise timing creates fairness and clearer prioritization.

options.text: A full transcript of jokes
Decisions, action items with owners and dates, and open questions
No actions so nobody is accountable
Only attendance emojis

questions.explanation: Notes are a clarity product for decisions and follow-through.

wrongExplanations.d: Attendance alone does not move work.

questions.prompt: Which standard captures the course’s end goal?

options.text: Write so a busy, well-meaning stranger can do the right next thing without a decoding meeting
Write to display vocabulary regardless of action
Write to win eloquence contests
Write to keep asks mysterious

questions.explanation: Reader-action clarity is the professional standard taught throughout.

wrongExplanations.b: Display writing is a listed mistake.
wrongExplanations.c: Eloquence is optional; clarity is not.
